paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea: no one is too far gone for God to hear. Manasseh led Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did "greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites" (2 Chronicles 33:9). Then, in his distress, he "earnestly humbled himself before the God of his fathers," and "the LORD received his plea and heard his petition" (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I'm telling you, the God who reached in and found me is the same God who heard a man in bronze shackles.

Now look at what humbling himself did for Manasseh. He came to know "that the LORD is God" (2 Chronicles 33:13), and then he got to work cleaning out what he had built (2 Chronicles 33:15-16). Real humility doesn't stop at "I'm sorry," friend. It turns around and starts hauling out the junk. And notice the people were only half-fixed (2 Chronicles 33:17), so I think that tells us one person's turning doesn't automatically carry everybody else along.

That brings us to Amon, because his story is the other warning. He did evil like his father, but he "did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done; instead, Amon increased his guilt" (2 Chronicles 33:23). A good ending in the family doesn't get handed down like a recipe card, so each of us has to humble ourselves for ourselves. So here's your cookie for the day, baker: if you've got something you're ashamed of, don't hide it, pray, because the door to God stays open to the humble, and that's why I keep my ovens ready.
